text: In discrete convolution, the new pixel is a {{c1::weighted sum}} of intensities in a neighbourhood. The weights come from a {{c2::kernel}} (also called a mask or filter).
extra: If the neighbourhood is centred on the pixel, its size must be odd, like \(3\times 3\) or \(5\times 5\).

text: Convolution at pixel \(P\): centre the kernel on \(P\), multiply each neighbour by its weight, {{c1::sum}} the products, then write that value into the {{c2::output}} image at \(P\).
extra: Keep a separate output buffer so you do not overwrite input pixels mid-pass.

text: Smoothing kernels are normalized so the coefficients sum to {{c1::1}}. That keeps the mean intensity steady in flat regions and avoids a brightness {{c2::bias}}.
extra: Study guide: sum of kernel weights equals 1. The scale factor is often written outside the matrix.

text: Practice: a \(3\times 3\) mean filter uses weights of 1 instead of \(1/9\) on an 8-bit image clipped to 0-255. The image gets about {{c1::nine times brighter}}, so most pixels slam into {{c2::255}}.
extra: Study-guide mini practice Q4 answer B. Relative weights alone do not save you when the sum is wrong.

text: Border strategy copy-of-input: where the kernel hangs off the edge, you {{c1::copy}} the input pixel into the output. Size stays the same, but you get an {{c2::unprocessed}} rim.
extra: Know size and border behaviour for each strategy on the midterm.

text: Border strategy truncation-of-image: drop every pixel where convolution cannot run. The output is {{c1::smaller}} than the input, and it is offset relative to it.
extra: Copy keeps the size and leaves a raw border. Truncation throws that border away.

text: Border strategy truncation-of-kernel: treat the edges as a special case and run a {{c1::modified}} kernel that only covers the pixels still inside the image.
extra: Corners and edges need different truncated kernels, so the code gets messy fast.

text: Reflected indexing maps an out-of-range coordinate by {{c1::mirroring}} it back into the image. The lecture calls this the most useful border option.
extra: Circular wrap pretends the image tiles forever, and it is rarely used for image processing.

text: Unsharp masking builds an edge image \(g(x,y)={{c1::f(x,y)-S(f(x,y)) }}\), where \(S(f)\) is a {{c2::blurred}} copy of \(f\).
extra: Subtracting the blur strips the low frequencies and leaves high-frequency detail.

text: Unsharp masking puts the edges back with \(f_{UM}(x,y)={{c1::f(x,y)+kg(x,y) }}\). Here \(g\) is the edge image and \(k\) scales how hard you sharpen.
extra: Study guide form: \(f_{UM}=f+k\cdot g\). Typical \(k\) is about 0.2 to 0.7.

text: In unsharp masking, cranking up \(k\) gives {{c1::more}} sharpening. When \(k>{{c2::1}}\), people sometimes call the method high-boost.
extra: Reasonable \(k\) values sit roughly between 0.2 and 0.7.

text: Gaussian smoothing uses the nonuniform weights \(w(i,j)={{c1::e^{-(i^2+j^2)/(2\sigma^2)} }}\). Larger \(\sigma\) means {{c2::more}} blur, because the hump spreads farther from the centre.
extra: Support is typically \(\pm 3\sigma\). The kernel is isotropic, so it has no directional bias.

text: A median filter replaces the pixel with the {{c1::middle-ranked}} value in its neighbourhood. It knocks out {{c2::impulse}} noise when the bad pixels are less than half the neighbourhood.
extra: It is a nonlinear order-statistic filter, not a weighted sum.

text: Unlike averaging, a median filter better preserves {{c1::sharp edges}}. Mean and Gaussian (larger \(\sigma\)) filters {{c2::blur}} edges while they quiet the noise.
extra: Median also wipes out real thin features that occupy less than half the neighbourhood.
